title: Solutions, Acids, Bases and Thermochemistry
bigQuestion: What decides whether a substance dissolves, how acidic a solution becomes, and whether a reaction will release heat and go forward on its own?

story.title: The Lake That Turned Sour
story.kicker: Rain that fell on the north woods was quietly killing fish, and the cause was smoke from hundreds of miles away.
paragraphs: In the 1970s, fishing guides on small lakes in northern Wisconsin and Michigan's Upper Peninsula began to notice something wrong. Lakes that had held trout and minnows for as long as anyone remembered were turning strangely clear. Clear water sounds healthy. It was not. The tiny floating life that clouds a lake was dying, and the fish were vanishing with it. When scientists dipped pH meters into the water, the reading was lower than it should have been. The lakes were turning acid.

The rain was the carrier. Normal rain is already slightly acidic, about pH 5.6, because carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in it. But rain across the eastern half of North America was arriving at pH 4.5, sometimes lower. Each whole number on the pH scale is a factor of ten, so that rain carried more than ten times the acid of clean rain. The acid was sulfuric and nitric, made in the sky from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. And those gases came out of tall smokestacks at coal-burning power plants, some of them in Illinois, where the coal underground is rich in sulfur.

Lake Michigan itself was never in danger. Its basin sits on limestone and dolomite, rock made of calcium carbonate, and carbonate reacts with acid and neutralizes it. The big lake is a buffer the size of a state. The small lakes to the north were different. They lie on granite and sand left behind by glaciers, with almost no carbonate to spare. Every acid rainstorm pushed their pH a little lower, and nothing pushed it back. Below about pH 5, aluminum leaches out of the soil and poisons fish gills. The trout went first.

To be sure of the cause, researchers in the 1980s divided one small Wisconsin lake in half with a plastic curtain and slowly added acid to one side while leaving the other alone. Over several years the acidified half lost species one after another, in the same order the sick lakes had. It was a controlled experiment on an entire ecosystem, and it settled the argument.

The fix was chemistry too. In 1990 Congress amended the Clean Air Act to cap sulfur dioxide from power plants. Plants installed scrubbers that spray limestone slurry through the smoke, so that the sulfur dioxide reacts to form gypsum, the same mineral in drywall. Others switched to low-sulfur coal from Wyoming. By 2020, sulfur dioxide from those plants had fallen by more than 90 percent. The rain grew cleaner. Many lakes have slowly recovered, though some are still short of carbonate decades later. Everything in this chapter, dissolving, pH, buffers, titration and the energy of reactions, is in that story.
story.think: Two lakes received the same acid rain for twenty years. One stayed healthy and the other lost its fish. What single difference in the ground beneath them could explain that?

lessons.title: Dissolving and Solubility
lessons.mainIdea: A substance dissolves when the attractions between solvent and solute particles are strong enough to pull the solute apart, and temperature and pressure change how much can dissolve.
reading: Stir a spoon of sugar into tea and it disappears. Stir in a spoon of sand and it sits on the bottom. Both are solids in water, yet one forms a *solution*, a uniform mixture of one substance spread through another, and the other does not. The dissolved substance is the *solute*; the substance doing the dissolving is the *solvent*. Water is the solvent in tea, in blood, in lakes and in nearly all of the chemistry of life.

Dissolving is a tug of war. Water molecules are polar, with a slightly negative oxygen end and slightly positive hydrogen ends. Table salt is a crystal of sodium ions and chloride ions. When water meets the crystal, the oxygen ends crowd around each sodium ion and the hydrogen ends around each chloride ion, and the pulls are strong enough to lift ions off the crystal one by one. Sugar molecules are not ions, but they carry polar groups that water grabs the same way. Oil has no such handles, so water leaves it alone. The rule of thumb is that like dissolves like: polar solvents dissolve polar and ionic solutes, and nonpolar solvents dissolve nonpolar ones.

Every solute has a limit. Keep adding salt to a glass of water and eventually the crystals stop disappearing. The solution is *saturated*. The maximum amount that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature is the *solubility*. For most solids, solubility rises with temperature, which is why hot tea holds more sugar than iced tea and why a cooling solution can suddenly drop crystals. Gases behave the other way. A warm soda goes flat faster because carbon dioxide is less soluble in warm water than in cold.

Pressure matters for gases too. A soda is bottled under several atmospheres of carbon dioxide, which forces far more gas into the liquid than air pressure could. Open the cap, the pressure drops, and the excess escapes as bubbles. The same law explains why a diver who rises too fast gets the bends: nitrogen dissolved in the blood at depth comes out of solution as the pressure falls. And it explains why a warming lake or ocean holds less dissolved oxygen, a problem for fish long before the water feels hot.

words.d: a uniform mixture in which one substance is spread evenly through another
the substance that dissolves in a solution, such as salt in salt water
the substance that does the dissolving, such as water in salt water
the most solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature
holding as much dissolved solute as possible at that temperature

look.title: The Fish Kill in August
look.text: A shallow Illinois pond loses hundreds of fish during a heat wave in August. The water is not polluted and no chemical was spilled. A biologist notes that the pond warmed to 32 degrees Celsius and that the fish died at dawn, after a still, cloudy night when the pond's plants were not producing oxygen.
look.prompt: Use what you know about gas solubility and temperature to explain the fish kill. Why did it happen at dawn rather than at noon?

check.q: Why does salt dissolve in water but oil does not?
choices: Water molecules are polar and pull ions apart, but have no strong attraction to nonpolar oil
Oil molecules are too small to be surrounded by water
Salt melts in water and oil does not
check.why: Like dissolves like. Water's polar ends grip ions and polar groups; oil offers nothing for them to grip.

check.q: What happens to the solubility of a gas in water as the water warms?
check.why: Gases are less soluble in warm water, which is why warm soda goes flat and warm lakes hold less oxygen.

check.q: A solution has as much sugar dissolved as it can hold at 20 degrees Celsius. What is it called?
check.why: A saturated solution holds the maximum solute for that temperature; any more will not dissolve.

lessons.title: Molarity and Dilution
lessons.mainIdea: Molarity, moles of solute per liter of solution, lets chemists measure out exact numbers of dissolved particles by volume.
reading: A recipe that says add some salt is useless to a chemist. So is one that says add 5 grams, because 5 grams of sodium chloride and 5 grams of sugar contain very different numbers of particles. Chemists describe *concentration* as *molarity*: moles of solute per liter of solution, written with a capital M. A 1.0 M salt solution has 1.0 mole, 58.44 grams, of sodium chloride in each liter. A 0.10 M solution has one tenth as much.

Making a solution of known molarity takes care. To prepare 1.0 liter of 0.50 M NaCl, weigh out 0.50 mole, about 29.2 grams. Dissolve it in less than a liter of water, then add water until the total volume reaches exactly 1.0 liter. The order matters. Dissolving salt changes the volume slightly, so you cannot simply add 29.2 grams to a full liter and expect 1.0 liter of solution. Chemists use a flask with a single line etched at the exact volume for this job.

Often a lab keeps one concentrated stock solution and dilutes it as needed. Adding water changes the volume but not the number of moles, so the moles before and after are equal. Since moles equal molarity times volume, M1 times V1 equals M2 times V2. To make 500 milliliters of 0.10 M acid from a 1.0 M stock, solve for V1: 0.10 times 500 divided by 1.0 equals 50 milliliters. Measure 50 milliliters of stock, add water to 500 milliliters, done.

Molarity connects solutions to stoichiometry. If you know the molarity and the volume, you know the moles, and moles are what the balanced equation counts. A nurse preparing a saline drip, a water plant adding chlorine, and a chemist neutralizing an acid spill all reason the same way: how many moles do I need, and what volume of this solution holds them?

words.d: how much solute is present in a given amount of solution
moles of solute per liter of solution, written M
adding solvent to a solution to lower its concentration without changing the moles of solute
a concentrated solution kept on hand and diluted to make weaker ones

look.title: The Two Beakers
look.text: Beaker A holds 100 milliliters of 2.0 M sugar solution. Beaker B holds 400 milliliters of 0.50 M sugar solution. A student says beaker A is more concentrated, so it must contain more sugar. Another says beaker B is bigger, so it must contain more sugar.
look.prompt: Calculate the moles of sugar in each beaker. Who is right, and what is the difference between concentration and amount?

check.q: How many moles of NaCl are in 2.0 L of a 0.25 M solution?
check.why: Moles equal molarity times volume: 0.25 times 2.0 equals 0.50 mole.

check.q: What volume of 6.0 M HCl is needed to make 300 mL of 1.0 M HCl?
check.why: M1V1 = M2V2: 6.0 times V1 equals 1.0 times 300, so V1 is 50 mL.

check.q: Why do chemists dissolve the solute first and then add water up to the final volume, rather than adding the solute to a full liter?
choices: Because the solute would not dissolve in a full liter
Because the solute must be heated first
Because dissolving changes the volume, so the final volume must be set after the solute is in
check.why: Adding solute changes the total volume. Only by filling to the mark last do you get exactly one liter of solution.

lessons.title: Salt on the Roads
lessons.mainIdea: Dissolved particles lower a solvent's freezing point and raise its boiling point by an amount that depends only on how many particles are dissolved, not what they are.
reading: Every winter, Chicago spreads tens of thousands of tons of salt on its streets. The salt does not melt ice by being warm. It works because a solution freezes at a lower temperature than the pure solvent. Dissolved particles get in the way when water molecules try to lock into the orderly pattern of ice, so the water must be colder before ice can form. This is *freezing point depression*, and it is one of a family of colligative properties, effects that depend on the number of dissolved particles rather than their identity.

The size of the effect is easy to estimate. For water, each mole of dissolved particles in a kilogram of water lowers the freezing point by about 1.86 degrees Celsius. Sodium chloride splits into two ions, so one mole of salt gives two moles of particles and about 3.7 degrees of depression. Calcium chloride, CaCl2, splits into three ions and works harder per mole, which is why road crews use it in the coldest weather. Seawater, with about 35 grams of dissolved salts per kilogram, freezes at about minus 1.9 degrees Celsius.

The same crowding raises the boiling point. Pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level; each mole of particles per kilogram raises that by about 0.51 degrees. A pot of salted pasta water boils only a fraction of a degree hotter, so the salt is for flavor, not speed. Antifreeze in a car radiator does both jobs at once: it keeps the coolant from freezing in January and from boiling in July.

Colligative properties gave nineteenth-century chemists a way to weigh molecules. Dissolve a known mass of an unknown substance, measure how far the freezing point drops, and you can compute how many moles you added and therefore the molar mass. When salt lowered the freezing point about twice as much as expected, it was a clue that salt breaks into two particles in water. Svante Arrhenius built his theory of ions on exactly such puzzles.

words.d: a property of a solution that depends on the number of dissolved particles, not their kind
the lowering of a solvent's freezing point by dissolved particles
the raising of a solvent's boiling point by dissolved particles
an atom or group of atoms with an electric charge, formed when a salt dissolves or an acid gives up hydrogen

look.title: Freezing Points of Water Solutions
look.cite: estimated from the freezing point constant of water, 1.86 °C per mole of particles per kg, rounded
look.prompt: Why does one mole of calcium chloride lower the freezing point about three times as much as one mole of sugar? What does that tell you about what happens to each solute in water?

check.q: Why does salt keep a wet road from freezing?
choices: Salt releases heat as it dissolves
Salt coats the ice and insulates it
Dissolved particles interfere with ice forming, so the water must get colder to freeze
check.why: Freezing point depression: solute particles get in the way of the orderly ice pattern, lowering the freezing temperature.

check.q: Which solution has the lowest freezing point?
choices: 1 mol of sugar per kg of water
1 mol of NaCl per kg of water
1 mol of CaCl2 per kg of water
They all freeze at the same temperature
check.why: Colligative effects depend on particle count. CaCl2 gives three ions per formula unit, more than NaCl's two or sugar's one.

check.q: Does adding a spoon of salt make pasta water boil noticeably faster?
choices: Yes, salt lowers the boiling point
Yes, salt makes the water heat up quicker
No, it raises the boiling point only by a fraction of a degree
No, salt has no effect on any property of water
check.why: A spoon of salt in a big pot is a small concentration, and boiling point elevation is only about 0.5 degrees per mole of particles per kg.

lessons.title: What Makes an Acid
lessons.mainIdea: An acid gives up a hydrogen ion and a base accepts one, and the strength of an acid is how completely it does so in water.
reading: Lemon juice, vinegar, and the fluid in your stomach share a sharp taste, a sting on a cut and the power to fizz on marble. They are acids. Soap, baking soda solution and household ammonia feel slippery and taste bitter. They are bases. For centuries chemists sorted substances this way by their effects. The modern definition explains the effects. An acid is a substance that donates a hydrogen ion, H+, which is just a bare proton. A base is a substance that accepts one.

Put hydrogen chloride gas in water and every HCl molecule hands its proton to a water molecule, forming a hydronium ion, H3O+, and a chloride ion. Chemists usually write H3O+ simply as H+ for short. Because HCl gives up essentially all of its protons, it is a *strong acid*. Sulfuric and nitric acids, the acids in acid rain, are strong too. Acetic acid in vinegar is different. Only about one molecule in a hundred donates its proton at any moment; the rest hold on. It is a *weak acid*. Strong and weak describe how completely an acid ionizes, not how concentrated it is. A dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid can be equally dangerous.

Bases work in reverse. Sodium hydroxide, lye, splits completely into sodium ions and hydroxide ions, OH-, and hydroxide grabs any proton it meets. That makes it a strong base. Ammonia, NH3, is a weak base: it pulls a proton off water to form NH4+ and OH-, but only a small fraction does so. When an acid meets a base, the proton moves from one to the other. H+ and OH- combine to make water, and the leftover ions form a salt. Acid plus base gives salt plus water: *neutralization*.

Water itself does a little of both. In pure water, a tiny fraction of molecules pass protons among themselves, so there is always a trace of H+ and OH-, one of each for every 550 million water molecules at room temperature. Add acid and H+ rises while OH- falls. Add base and the reverse. Their product stays fixed. That balance is the reason a single scale, pH, can describe both acids and bases.

words.d: a substance that donates hydrogen ions (protons) in water
a substance that accepts hydrogen ions; many release hydroxide ions in water
an acid that gives up essentially all of its hydrogen ions in water, such as HCl
an acid that gives up only a small fraction of its hydrogen ions in water, such as acetic acid
the reaction of an acid with a base to form water and a salt

look.title: Arrhenius and the Idea of Ions, 1887
look.text: Arrhenius argued that when acids, bases and salts dissolve in water they split into electrically charged particles, and that the properties acids share come from the hydrogen ions they release. Many senior chemists found the idea of charged atoms floating free in water hard to accept, and his doctoral examiners gave the thesis a low grade.
look.cite: Svante Arrhenius, On the Dissociation of Substances Dissolved in Water, 1887 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What evidence from freezing points and from electrical conductivity could have convinced skeptics that dissolved salt really does split into ions?

check.q: What does an acid do in water?
check.why: By the modern definition, an acid is a proton donor; it hands H+ to water to form H3O+.

check.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
choices: Strong means a high molarity; concentrated means it ionizes fully
Strong means it ionizes almost completely; concentrated means a lot of it per liter
Strong acids are always safe when concentrated
check.why: Strength is about how completely an acid gives up protons. Concentration is about how much acid is dissolved.

check.q: What forms when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
check.why: Neutralization: H+ and OH- make water, and the remaining Na+ and Cl- make the salt sodium chloride.

lessons.title: The pH Scale
lessons.mainIdea: pH measures hydrogen ion concentration on a logarithmic scale, so each step of one pH unit means a tenfold change in acidity.
reading: Hydrogen ion concentrations in everyday solutions range over a trillion-fold, from stomach acid to lye. Writing those numbers out is clumsy, so in 1909 the Danish chemist Soren Sorensen, working at a brewery laboratory, proposed a shortcut. Take the hydrogen ion concentration in moles per liter and find the power of ten. Flip the sign. That is *pH*. A solution with H+ at 0.01 M, which is 10 to the minus 2, has pH 2. Pure water, with H+ at 10 to the minus 7 M, has pH 7.

The scale runs backward from what people expect: lower pH means more acid. And because it is *logarithmic*, each step of one unit is a factor of ten. Rain at pH 4.6 holds ten times the hydrogen ions of rain at pH 5.6, and rain at pH 3.6 holds a hundred times as much. A drop of pH from 8.2 to 8.1 sounds tiny, but it is a 26 percent increase in hydrogen ions. Chemists say a solution is acidic below 7, basic above 7 and *neutral* at 7, at least at room temperature.

You can measure pH in two ways. An *indicator* is a dye that changes color at a particular pH. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base; phenolphthalein is colorless in acid and pink in base; the juice of red cabbage runs through a whole rainbow. A pH meter uses a glass electrode whose voltage depends on the hydrogen ion concentration, and it reads to a hundredth of a unit. Field scientists carry both.

The scale is not limited to 0 through 14. Very concentrated strong acids can drop below 0 and very strong bases can rise above 14, though ordinary life stays inside that range. Your blood holds close to pH 7.4, your stomach near pH 2, and a swimming pool near 7.5. A change of a few tenths in your blood would be a medical emergency, which is why the next lesson matters.

words.d: a measure of hydrogen ion concentration; the negative power of ten of the H+ concentration in mol/L
a scale in which each step is a multiple, here tenfold, rather than an equal amount
a dye that changes color at a certain pH
neither acidic nor basic; pH 7 at room temperature, where H+ and OH- are equal

look.title: Approximate pH of Familiar Liquids
look.prompt: How many times more hydrogen ions does lemon juice hold than black coffee? Why is clean rain slightly acidic even without pollution?

check.q: A solution has a hydrogen ion concentration of 0.001 M. What is its pH?
check.why: 0.001 is 10 to the minus 3, so the pH is 3.

check.q: How does rain at pH 4 compare with rain at pH 6?
choices: It has 2 times as many hydrogen ions
It has half as many hydrogen ions
It has 20 times as many hydrogen ions
It has 100 times as many hydrogen ions
check.why: Each pH unit is a factor of ten, so two units is a factor of one hundred.

check.q: Which of these would turn phenolphthalein pink?
check.why: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acid and neutral solutions and turns pink in a basic solution such as sodium hydroxide.

lessons.title: Buffers
lessons.mainIdea: A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its partner base that soaks up added acid or base, holding pH nearly steady.
reading: Your blood receives acid all day long. Every cell dumps carbon dioxide into it, and carbon dioxide dissolved in water is an acid. Exercise floods it with lactic acid. Yet blood pH stays between about 7.35 and 7.45, and drifting outside that range by a few tenths is fatal. Something is absorbing the acid. That something is a *buffer*, and buffers are among the most important ideas in biology and environmental chemistry.

A buffer is a solution containing a weak acid together with its *conjugate base*, the particle left when the acid gives up its proton. Carbonic acid, H2CO3, and bicarbonate ion, HCO3-, form the main buffer in blood. Add acid, and bicarbonate grabs the extra protons, turning into carbonic acid. Add base, and carbonic acid hands over protons to neutralize it, turning into bicarbonate. Either way, the hydrogen ion concentration barely moves, because the added acid or base is converted into more of one buffer partner and less of the other.

A buffer has a capacity. It works only as long as both partners remain. Pour in enough acid to use up all the bicarbonate and the pH crashes. That is what happened to the northern lakes. Dissolved bicarbonate from the small amount of carbonate in their watersheds buffered the first years of acid rain, so the lakes seemed fine. When the bicarbonate ran out, the pH fell fast. Limestone-bedded lakes like Lake Michigan never ran out, because the rock itself keeps supplying carbonate.

Chemists design buffers for a chosen pH by picking a weak acid whose natural tendency to ionize lands near that value, then mixing it with roughly equal amounts of its conjugate base. Aquariums, swimming pools, shampoo, intravenous fluids and the enzyme reactions in every test tube in a biology lab all rely on a buffer chosen this way. The ocean is buffered by the same carbonate system as blood, and the last section of this chapter is about what happens when that buffer is pushed.

words.d: a solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists changes in pH
the particle that remains after an acid gives up its proton, such as bicarbonate from carbonic acid
the amount of acid or base a buffer can absorb before its pH changes sharply
the ion HCO3-, the main acid-absorbing partner in blood and in lake and ocean water

look.title: Two Beakers of Acid Rain
look.text: A student sets up two beakers of distilled water, each adjusted to pH 7. Into one she stirs a spoon of crushed limestone. She then adds drops of dilute sulfuric acid to both, ten drops at a time, checking pH after each round. The plain water drops from 7 to about 3 within twenty drops. The limestone beaker sits near pH 7 through a hundred drops before it slowly begins to fall.
look.prompt: Explain what the limestone is doing to the added acid. What does the eventual fall in the second beaker tell you about buffer capacity?

check.q: What two things does a buffer solution contain?
choices: A strong acid and a strong base
A weak acid and its conjugate base
A salt and a strong acid
check.why: The weak acid absorbs added base and the conjugate base absorbs added acid, so pH holds steady.

check.q: Why did some northern lakes seem healthy for years and then turn acid quickly?
choices: The acid rain suddenly got much stronger
The fish adapted, then died of old age
Their bicarbonate buffer held the pH until it was used up
check.why: A buffer has a capacity. Once the dissolved bicarbonate was consumed, nothing absorbed new acid and the pH fell fast.

check.q: What happens when acid is added to a bicarbonate buffer?
choices: Bicarbonate accepts the protons and becomes carbonic acid
Carbon dioxide gas is absorbed from the air
check.why: The conjugate base, bicarbonate, takes up the added H+, so the free hydrogen ion concentration barely changes.

lessons.title: Titration
lessons.mainIdea: In a titration, a solution of known concentration is added to one of unknown concentration until they exactly neutralize, and the volume used reveals the unknown.
reading: A bottle of vinegar claims to be 5 percent acetic acid. How would you check? You cannot see acid molecules, but you can count them by neutralizing them. Measure out a known volume of vinegar. Add a few drops of phenolphthalein. Then, from a long graduated tube called a *burette*, add sodium hydroxide solution of known molarity, drop by drop. Each hydroxide ion neutralizes one acetic acid molecule. The instant the last acid molecule is gone, the next drop of base makes the solution basic and the indicator flashes pink. This is *titration*.

The moment when the moles of base added exactly equal the moles of acid present is the *equivalence point*. The color change that signals it is the *endpoint*, and a good indicator is chosen so the two nearly coincide. Now the arithmetic is stoichiometry. Suppose 25.0 milliliters of vinegar needed 20.9 milliliters of 1.00 M NaOH. Moles of base equals 1.00 times 0.0209 liters, 0.0209 mole. Acetic acid and NaOH react one to one, so the vinegar held 0.0209 mole of acid in 25.0 milliliters, which is 0.836 M. Multiply by 60.05 grams per mole and you get about 50 grams of acetic acid per liter, close to 5 percent.

The shape of a titration matters as much as the endpoint. Plot pH against volume of base added and you get a curve that rises slowly, then leaps several units in a single drop near the equivalence point, then levels off. For a strong acid and strong base, the leap passes through pH 7. For a weak acid like acetic acid, the equivalence point sits above 7, because the conjugate base left behind is itself slightly basic. That is why phenolphthalein, which changes around pH 8 to 10, is the right choice for vinegar.

Titration is how water plants check alkalinity, how food chemists measure the acid in juice, and how environmental scientists measured the buffer capacity of lakes during the acid rain years. A lake sample titrated with acid tells you exactly how much more acid rain it can absorb before its pH falls. Those numbers, lake by lake, drew the map of which waters were in danger.

words.d: adding a solution of known concentration to one of unknown concentration until they exactly react
a tall graduated tube with a valve, used to add measured volumes of liquid drop by drop
the point in a titration when the moles of added reactant exactly match the moles present
the point at which the indicator changes color, chosen to fall close to the equivalence point

look.title: The Overshot Endpoint
look.text: A student titrates 20.0 milliliters of an unknown acid with 0.100 M NaOH. She is talking to a friend and does not close the burette valve in time. The solution turns deep pink, not faint pink, and the burette reads 24.6 milliliters when she looks. Her lab partner recorded that the first hint of pink appeared at 22.1 milliliters.
look.prompt: Which volume should she use for her calculation, and why? Would her mistake make the calculated concentration of the acid too high or too low?

check.q: What is the equivalence point of a titration?
choices: The point where the indicator is added
The point where the burette is empty
The point where the pH reaches 14
The point where moles of base added equal moles of acid present
check.why: At the equivalence point the reactants have exactly neutralized each other; the indicator's color change is meant to mark it.

check.q: It takes 30.0 mL of 0.200 M NaOH to neutralize 15.0 mL of HCl. What is the molarity of the HCl?
check.why: Moles of base are 0.200 times 0.0300, or 0.00600 mole. HCl reacts one to one, so 0.00600 mole in 0.0150 L is 0.400 M.

check.q: Why is the equivalence point of a weak acid titrated with a strong base above pH 7?
choices: Because the conjugate base left behind is slightly basic
Because weak acids are more concentrated
Because some acid always remains unreacted
check.why: When all the weak acid has been converted to its conjugate base, that base pulls a few protons off water, leaving the solution slightly basic.

lessons.title: Measuring Heat
lessons.mainIdea: The heat a reaction releases or absorbs, its enthalpy change, can be measured by tracking the temperature change of a known mass of water.
reading: Crack a chemical hand warmer and it grows hot for hours. Squeeze an instant cold pack and it turns icy in seconds. Both are reactions, one that releases heat and one that absorbs it. A reaction that releases heat to its surroundings is *exothermic*; one that draws heat in is *endothermic*. Chemists measure the heat of a reaction at constant pressure as its *enthalpy change*, written delta H. Exothermic reactions have negative delta H, because the system loses energy; endothermic reactions have positive delta H.

To measure it, you let the reaction warm or cool a known amount of water and watch the thermometer. Water needs 4.18 joules to raise one gram by one degree Celsius; that number is its *specific heat*. Heat equals mass times specific heat times temperature change, q = m c delta T. If a reaction warms 100 grams of water by 5.0 degrees, it released 100 times 4.18 times 5.0, about 2,090 joules, or 2.09 kilojoules. A foam cup with a lid and a thermometer is a perfectly good *calorimeter* for a school lab.

Divide the heat by the moles that reacted and you have delta H per mole, a number that belongs to the reaction itself. Burning one mole of methane, 16 grams, releases about 890 kilojoules. Burning one mole of glucose, the sugar your cells use, releases about 2,800 kilojoules whether it burns in a flame or is broken down slowly in your body. Dissolving one mole of ammonium nitrate, the salt in many cold packs, absorbs about 26 kilojoules, which is why the pack turns cold.

The first careful calorimeter was built in 1783 by Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace. They put a guinea pig in a chamber surrounded by ice and weighed the meltwater. The animal's body heat melted ice at about the rate that burning charcoal did for the same carbon dioxide produced. It was the first quantitative evidence that respiration is a slow form of combustion, and it was done with nothing more than ice, a balance and a good idea.

words.d: a reaction that releases heat to its surroundings; delta H is negative
a reaction that absorbs heat from its surroundings; delta H is positive
delta H, the heat absorbed or released by a reaction at constant pressure
the heat needed to raise one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius; 4.18 J for water
an insulated container used to measure heat by the temperature change of a known mass

look.title: Heat Released by Burning One Mole
look.cite: standard enthalpies of combustion, rounded reference values
look.prompt: Hydrogen releases the least heat per mole but the most per gram. Show why, using molar masses, and explain why rockets care about heat per gram.

check.q: A reaction warms 200 grams of water by 3.0 degrees Celsius. How much heat did it release?
check.why: q = m c delta T = 200 times 4.18 times 3.0, about 2,508 joules.

check.q: A cold pack turns cold when squeezed. Which describes its reaction?
check.why: The pack draws heat from its surroundings, including your hand, so the reaction absorbs energy: endothermic, delta H positive.

check.q: What did the Lavoisier–Laplace ice calorimeter measure?
choices: The mass of ice melted by the heat of a guinea pig or a burning fuel
The volume of oxygen an animal breathed
The pH of an animal's blood
check.why: Heat melted the surrounding ice, and the mass of meltwater measured the heat, linking respiration to combustion.

lessons.title: Hess's Law
lessons.mainIdea: Because enthalpy depends only on the starting and ending substances, the heat of a reaction can be found by adding the heats of steps that lead to the same result.
reading: Some reactions cannot be measured directly. Carbon burning to carbon monoxide, C + half O2 gives CO, always makes some carbon dioxide too, so no calorimeter can isolate it. In 1840 the Swiss-Russian chemist Germain Hess found the way around. The heat of a reaction, he showed, is the same whether the reaction happens in one step or in several. Only the start and end matter. This is *Hess's law*, and it follows from the fact that enthalpy is a *state function*, a property that depends on the current state and not on the path taken to reach it.

Altitude is a state function. Climb a mountain by the steep trail or the winding road and your gain in height is the same. Distance walked is not a state function; the road is longer. Enthalpy is like altitude. So if you can measure two reactions that together add up to the one you want, add their heats. Carbon to carbon dioxide releases 393.5 kilojoules per mole. Carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide releases 283.0. Subtract, and carbon to carbon monoxide must release 393.5 minus 283.0, which is 110.5 kilojoules per mole. No one has ever measured it directly, and every chemist trusts the number.

The rules for adding equations are simple. Reverse an equation and flip the sign of delta H. Multiply an equation by a number and multiply delta H by the same number. Then add the equations, canceling anything that appears on both sides. Chemists have tabulated the enthalpy of forming each compound from its elements, the *standard enthalpy of formation*, so that the heat of any reaction can be computed as the formation enthalpies of products minus those of reactants.

Hess's law is the reason a food label can state calories without burning your lunch. The energy in a sandwich is the sum of the energies of its carbohydrates, fats and proteins, each measured once in a calorimeter. It is also why engineers can predict the heat of a rocket fuel that has never been tested, and why the total energy of a hand warmer can be worked out from a table before it is built.

words.d: the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in several
a property, such as enthalpy or altitude, that depends only on the current state, not on the path
the heat change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states

look.title: Hess on the Constant Sum of Heat, 1840
look.text: Hess reported that when a chemical compound is formed, the total heat given off is constant, whether the compound is made directly or through a series of intermediate steps. He had measured the heat released when sulfuric acid was diluted with water in one stage or in several, and found the sum the same.
look.cite: Germain Hess, Annalen der Physik und Chemie, 1840 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why does Hess's result require that enthalpy be a state function? What would it mean if two different paths gave different total heats?

check.q: Which is a state function?
choices: The distance you walk to school
The enthalpy change of a reaction
The number of steps in a reaction
check.why: Enthalpy depends only on the starting and ending states, like altitude, not on the route between them.

check.q: If a reaction releases 100 kJ, what is delta H for the reverse reaction?
check.why: Reversing a reaction flips the sign of delta H, so the reverse absorbs 100 kJ.

check.q: C to CO2 releases 393.5 kJ/mol and CO to CO2 releases 283.0 kJ/mol. What is delta H for C to CO?
check.why: By Hess's law, subtract: 393.5 minus 283.0 equals 110.5 kJ released, so delta H is -110.5 kJ/mol.

lessons.title: Entropy and Free Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Whether a reaction goes forward on its own depends on both the heat it releases and the disorder it creates, combined in the free energy change.
reading: Not every reaction that releases heat happens, and some reactions that absorb heat happen anyway. Ice melts in a warm room even though melting absorbs heat. A cold pack works even though it makes itself colder. Heat alone cannot be the whole story. The missing piece is *entropy*, a measure of how spread out energy and matter are, roughly, how many ways the particles can be arranged. Gas has more entropy than liquid, liquid more than solid, and a mixture more than the pure substances separated.

Nature favors two things: lower energy and higher entropy. Sometimes they agree. Burning methane releases heat and turns one gas molecule plus two into one plus two, so both push forward. Sometimes they conflict. Melting ice raises energy but also raises entropy, because liquid water molecules can arrange themselves in far more ways than ice. Which one wins depends on temperature. Above 0 degrees Celsius entropy wins and ice melts. Below it, energy wins and water freezes.

In the 1870s the American physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs put the two together into a single number, the *free energy* change: delta G equals delta H minus T times delta S, where T is kelvin temperature and delta S is the entropy change. If delta G is negative, the reaction is *spontaneous*: it can go forward on its own. If delta G is positive, it cannot, though the reverse can. Multiplying entropy by temperature is what makes heat matter more in the cold and disorder matter more in the heat. For melting ice, delta H is about 6.0 kilojoules per mole and delta S about 22 joules per mole-kelvin, and delta G crosses zero at 6,000 divided by 22, about 273 K. That is 0 degrees Celsius, exactly where it should be.

Spontaneous does not mean fast. Diamond turning to graphite is spontaneous and takes longer than the age of Earth. Gasoline reacting with air is spontaneous and waits for a spark. Free energy says whether a reaction can happen and how far it will go. Rate, from the last chapter, says how long it takes. Living cells run reactions with positive delta G all the time, but only by coupling them to reactions with larger negative delta G, chiefly the breakdown of glucose, so that the total is still downhill.

words.d: a measure of how spread out energy and matter are; the number of ways particles can be arranged
delta G, which combines enthalpy and entropy to predict whether a reaction can go forward on its own
able to happen on its own without continued outside input; delta G is negative
a reaction that cannot go on its own but is driven by a linked reaction with a larger negative delta G

look.title: The Cold Pack Puzzle
look.text: An instant cold pack contains ammonium nitrate and a pouch of water. Squeeze it, the salt dissolves, and the pack drops well below room temperature within a minute. A student objects that this should be impossible: the process absorbs heat, so it moves to higher energy, and things are not supposed to roll uphill.
look.prompt: Explain, using entropy and the equation for delta G, how a process that absorbs heat can still be spontaneous. What has increased in disorder when a crystal dissolves?

check.q: Which has the highest entropy?
check.why: Gas molecules move freely and can be arranged in the most ways, so vapor has the most entropy.

check.q: A reaction has a negative delta G. What does that mean?
choices: It can go forward on its own
check.why: Negative delta G means spontaneous: the reaction can proceed without outside input, though it says nothing about speed.

check.q: Why does ice melt above 0 degrees Celsius but not below?
choices: Above 0 the entropy gain outweighs the heat absorbed; below 0 it does not
Delta H changes sign at 0 degrees
Ice has more entropy than water above 0 degrees
Melting releases heat only above 0 degrees
check.why: T times delta S grows with temperature. Above 273 K it exceeds delta H, making delta G negative and melting spontaneous.

lessons.title: The Ocean's Changing pH
lessons.mainIdea: Carbon dioxide dissolving in seawater forms carbonic acid, and the ocean's surface pH has dropped measurably as atmospheric carbon dioxide has risen.
reading: The ocean is the largest buffered solution on Earth, and it is being titrated. Every year the burning of coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, and the ocean absorbs roughly a quarter to a third of it. When carbon dioxide dissolves in water, some of it becomes carbonic acid, H2CO3, which gives up protons to form bicarbonate and carbonate ions. More carbon dioxide means more protons. Measurements since the late 1980s, along with estimates from before industry, show the average pH of surface seawater has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1.

One tenth of a pH unit sounds trivial. Because the scale is logarithmic, it is roughly a 30 percent increase in hydrogen ion concentration, and it has happened faster than any change in the ocean's chemistry that geologists can find for millions of years. The ocean is still basic, with a pH above 7, so scientists call the process *ocean acidification*: the water is becoming less basic, moving toward acid, not becoming acid.

The chemistry that matters most to living things is the carbonate ion. Corals, clams, oysters, sea snails and the tiny drifting organisms at the base of ocean food webs build shells of calcium carbonate, CaCO3, and they need dissolved carbonate ions to do it. Added protons grab carbonate ions to form bicarbonate, so acidification lowers the carbonate available. Laboratory studies and field measurements show shells forming more slowly, and in some cold waters, where carbon dioxide is most soluble, thin shells beginning to dissolve. Oyster hatcheries on the U.S. Pacific coast were among the first businesses to notice, when larvae began failing in the 2000s.

This is the same chemistry as the acid lakes, run at a different scale. Both involve a carbonate buffer being consumed by added acid. The lakes got sulfuric acid from smokestacks; the ocean is getting carbonic acid from the air. And both have the same kind of remedy: reduce the source. The ocean's enormous buffer capacity means it will not become truly acidic, but the organisms that depend on carbonate live at the margin of that buffer, and the margin is where the change is felt.

words.d: the ongoing drop in ocean pH as the water absorbs carbon dioxide from the air
H2CO3, the weak acid formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water
CO3 with a 2- charge, the building block that shell-forming organisms need from seawater
CaCO3, the mineral of limestone, shells and coral, which reacts with acid

look.title: NOAA on a Changing Ocean
look.text: NOAA explains that the ocean absorbs about 30 percent of the carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere, and that as the water takes up more carbon dioxide its pH decreases. The agency reports that surface ocean pH has already dropped by about 0.1 unit since the start of the industrial era, an increase of roughly 30 percent in acidity, and that this change affects organisms that build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate.
look.cite: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, ocean acidification overview (paraphrased)
look.prompt: NOAA says pH fell 0.1 unit and acidity rose about 30 percent. Show how both statements can be true, using what you know about the pH scale.

check.q: What acid forms when carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater?
check.why: CO2 plus H2O gives H2CO3, carbonic acid, a weak acid that releases protons into the water.

check.q: The ocean's pH is about 8.1. Why do scientists still call the change acidification?
choices: Because the ocean's pH is below 7
Because the pH is moving toward the acidic direction, even though the water is still basic
Because the deep ocean is strongly acidic
check.why: Acidification names the direction of change. Seawater is becoming less basic, not becoming an acid.

check.q: Why does added acid make it harder for oysters to build shells?
choices: The acid dissolves the oysters' food
Protons combine with carbonate ions, leaving fewer for shell building
check.why: Added H+ converts carbonate to bicarbonate, so the carbonate ions that calcium carbonate shells require become scarcer.

lessons.title: Cleaning the Rain
lessons.mainIdea: Acid rain was reduced by removing sulfur dioxide from smoke through neutralization chemistry and by rules that capped total emissions.
reading: The name acid rain is older than the problem people remember. In 1872 the Scottish chemist Robert Angus Smith, studying the air of industrial Manchester, England, wrote about rain made acid by the sulfur in coal smoke and coined the term. For a century the damage stayed local: blackened stone, corroded iron. Then power plants built tall stacks to send the smoke away from cities, and the acid traveled hundreds of miles instead. Coal from the Illinois Basin is high in sulfur, and burning it makes sulfur dioxide, SO2. In the air, SO2 reacts with oxygen and water to become sulfuric acid, H2SO4, a strong acid.

The chemical fix is neutralization on an industrial scale. A *scrubber* sprays a slurry of ground limestone, calcium carbonate, into the flue gas. Sulfur dioxide, an acidic gas, reacts with the carbonate to form calcium sulfite, and oxygen in the gas converts most of it to calcium sulfate, gypsum. The same reaction that makes lemon juice fizz on marble turns poison into wallboard. A large scrubber removes more than 90 percent of the sulfur dioxide from a plant's smoke. Nitrogen oxides, the other source of acid rain, are cut with catalysts and with burners designed to run cooler.

The policy fix was a cap. The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments set a national ceiling on sulfur dioxide from power plants and issued permits, one per ton, that could be bought and sold. A plant that cut emissions cheaply could sell its spare permits to one that could not. The cap fell over time. Companies chose among scrubbers, low-sulfur coal from Wyoming and Montana, and eventually natural gas. By 2020, sulfur dioxide from those plants was down more than 90 percent from 1990, at a cost far below the early forecasts. Chicago's last two coal plants, Fisk and Crawford, closed in 2012.

Recovery has been slower than the cleanup. Rain over the Midwest and Northeast is far less acidic than it was, but many lakes lost so much buffering that their carbonate is still being rebuilt from the slow weathering of rock. Some have been limed by hand, tons of crushed limestone dumped from boats or helicopters, which is a titration in reverse. Fish have returned to many waters. The lesson for the ocean is the same as for the lakes: buffers can be spent, and the cheapest cure is to stop adding the acid.

words.d: rain made more acidic than normal by sulfuric and nitric acids formed from air pollution
SO2, a gas from burning sulfur-rich coal that becomes sulfuric acid in the air
equipment that removes sulfur dioxide from smoke by reacting it with limestone slurry
a rule that limits total emissions and lets permits to emit be bought and sold
adding crushed limestone to an acidified lake or soil to neutralize the acid

look.title: Smith Names Acid Rain, 1872
look.text: Smith reported that the rain falling on Manchester and other manufacturing towns contained free sulfuric acid, which he traced to the sulfur in the coal burned there, and that the acid in the air attacked stone, bleached fabrics and corroded metal. He used the phrase acid rain to describe it.
look.cite: Robert Angus Smith, Air and Rain: The Beginnings of a Chemical Climatology, 1872 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Smith found the acid near the factories. What change in how smoke was released, decades later, moved the damage to lakes hundreds of miles away?

check.q: What reaction takes place inside a limestone scrubber?
choices: Sulfur dioxide burns to form carbon dioxide
An acidic gas is neutralized by calcium carbonate
Limestone dissolves in sulfuric acid to release oxygen
Nitrogen gas is converted to fertilizer
check.why: Sulfur dioxide is an acidic gas; carbonate neutralizes it, forming calcium sulfite and then gypsum.

check.q: How did tall smokestacks change the acid rain problem?
choices: They removed the sulfur from the smoke
They made the smoke less acidic
They cooled the smoke so acid could not form
They spread the pollution over lakes hundreds of miles away
check.why: Tall stacks lifted the smoke into winds that carried it far from the source, turning a local nuisance into a regional problem.

check.q: Why has lake recovery lagged behind the drop in acid rain?
choices: Buffering carbonate is rebuilt only slowly by weathering of rock
The rain is still as acidic as before
Fish cannot return to a lake once they leave
Limestone scrubbers add acid to lakes
check.why: Acid rain consumed the lakes' bicarbonate. Replacing it depends on slow weathering, unless people add limestone directly.

review.q: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.50 mole of sugar in enough water to make 0.25 L?
review.why: Molarity is moles per liter: 0.50 divided by 0.25 equals 2.0 M.

review.q: Why does calcium chloride lower water's freezing point more than an equal number of moles of sugar?
choices: Sugar does not dissolve in cold water
It releases heat as it dissolves
It splits into three ions, giving three times as many particles
review.why: Colligative properties depend on particle count, and each CaCl2 unit gives three ions in solution.

review.q: A solution has pH 9. Which statement is true?
choices: It has 100 times more H+ than pure water
Its H+ concentration is 10 to the minus 9 M
review.why: pH 9 means the hydrogen ion concentration is 10 to the minus 9 M; that is basic, less H+ than pure water.

review.q: What does a buffer do when a small amount of strong acid is added?
choices: Turns the acid into a base
Lowers the pH by exactly one unit
Absorbs the added protons so the pH changes very little
review.why: The conjugate base in the buffer takes up the added H+, holding pH nearly steady until the buffer's capacity is used up.

review.q: In a titration, 10.0 mL of 0.50 M NaOH neutralizes 20.0 mL of an acid that reacts one to one. What is the acid's molarity?
review.why: Moles of base are 0.50 times 0.0100, or 0.0050 mole. That many moles of acid in 0.0200 L is 0.25 M.

review.q: Which sign of delta H describes a reaction that warms its surroundings?
review.why: An exothermic reaction releases heat, so the system loses energy and delta H is negative.

review.q: A reaction absorbs heat but is still spontaneous at room temperature. What must be true?
choices: Its entropy increases enough that T times delta S exceeds delta H
review.why: Delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. A positive delta H can still give negative delta G if the entropy increase is large enough.

review.q: Why did Lake Michigan stay safe from acid rain while nearby small lakes turned acid?
choices: Lake Michigan is too deep for rain to affect
Its limestone bedrock supplies carbonate that neutralizes acid
Acid rain fell only on Wisconsin
The small lakes had more fish to produce acid
review.why: Calcium carbonate in the lake's basin acts as a buffer with enormous capacity; the granite-bedded lakes had almost none.
